ECE 6390 / Orbits and look angles

GEO & rotating Earth

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how a satellite can move rapidly in space while remaining at one position in an observer’s sky.

An inertial frame describes the orbital motion around Earth. An Earth-fixed frame rotates eastward at angular rate ωₑ. For a circular equatorial prograde orbit, the relative longitude rate is n − ωₑ.

Geostationary motion requires a circular equatorial prograde orbit with n = ωₑ. Matching only the period produces geosynchronous motion; eccentricity or inclination can still make the satellite move in the sky.

Use the sidereal rotation period, approximately 86,164 s, when matching an inertial orbit to Earth's rotation. Changing frames changes coordinates and relative rates; the physical gravitational motion remains the same.

Example

If n − ωₑ = 10⁻⁶ rad/s, the Earth-fixed longitude changes by 0.01 rad, about 0.573°, in 10,000 s.

    Practice

    1. A satellite has the sidereal orbital period but an inclined orbit. Does it remain geostationary? Explain which condition is missing.

    Separate matching the rotation rate from keeping the subpoint on the equator.

    It is geosynchronous, but its subpoint moves north and south because the orbital plane is inclined. A geostationary orbit also needs zero inclination, zero eccentricity, and prograde motion.
